subject: Biotechnology
title: Disease Resistance Genes
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Disease Resistance Genes.

hook.text: Late blight destroyed Ireland's potato crop in 1845 — the same disease still costs $6 billion per year globally.

buildup.text: Wild potato relatives carry natural resistance genes — but crossing them into cultivated varieties takes decades.

discovery.text: Cisgenic potatoes carry resistance genes from wild relatives via genetic engineering — same species, faster transfer.

twist.text: Pathogens evolve to overcome single resistance genes — stacking three or more genes provides durable protection.

climax.text: The Desiree potato with three stacked R genes resisted late blight for over five years in field trials.

punchline.text: Wild genes, engineered delivery — stacking resistance outpaces the pathogen.

quiz.question: Why is stacking multiple resistance genes more effective than using one?
options: Each gene produces a different toxin that kills the pathogen
Pathogens must overcome all resistance mechanisms simultaneously, which is extremely unlikely
Stacked genes make the plant grow faster and outcompete disease

details.summary: Disease resistance genes in plants recognize pathogen molecules and trigger immune responses that halt infection. Biotechnology identifies, isolates, and transfers these resistance genes between species to protect crops from devastating bacterial, fungal, and viral diseases.
details.whyItMatters: Plant diseases destroy 10 to 16 percent of global crop production annually. Engineering durable disease resistance reduces massive yield losses and decreases dependence on chemical fungicides that harm ecosystems.
takeaways: R genes encode receptors that detect specific pathogen molecules
Gene stacking combines multiple resistance genes for durable protection
CRISPR can activate dormant resistance pathways already in crop genomes

faq.question: Why do disease resistance genes stop working over time?
faq.answer: Pathogens evolve rapidly and can mutate the molecules that R genes detect, overcoming single-gene resistance in as few as three to five years. Stacking multiple R genes targeting different pathogen components makes it much harder for pathogens to overcome all defenses.

faq.question: Can disease resistance be transferred between unrelated plant species?
faq.answer: Yes. Resistance genes from wild relatives or entirely different species can be transferred into crops using genetic engineering. For example, a resistance gene from peppers has been successfully transferred to tomatoes to protect against bacterial spot disease.
